BLACK FRIDAY SALES ANALYSIS¶

Project objective¶

  • Who are the customers?
  • Which demographic groups purchase more?
  • Which product categories generate more revenue?
  • Which customers are high-value customers?
  • Does gender affect purchasing behavior?
  • Does marital status affect purchasing behavior?
  • Which cities contribute more to sales?
  • What products are commonly purchased together?
  • What business strategies can be recommended?

ABOUT DATASET:¶

Dataset: Black Friday Sales Analysis

  • Number of Rows : 550068
  • Number of Columns : 12
  • Columns Include : User_ID,Product_ID,Gender,Age,Occupation,City_Category, Stay_In_Current_City_Years, Marital_Status,Product_Category_1,Product_Category_2, Product_Category_3 and Purchase.

Data Overview

The first step is to get a quick overview of the dataset. This gives an initial understanding of the dataset's structure, including the number of rows, columns, data types, sample data, and basic statistics.

Converted category columns to string as they are categorical variables. Replaced missing values in Category 2 & 3 with "Unknown" to preserve missing information.

Outlier Analysis¶

In [21]:
# Identify outliers
Q1 = df["Purchase"].quantile(0.25)
Q3 = df["Purchase"].quantile(0.75)

IQR = Q3 - Q1

lower_limit = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper_limit = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

print("Q1:", Q1)
print("Q3:", Q3)
print("IQR:", IQR)
print("Lower Limit:", lower_limit)
print("Upper Limit:", upper_limit)

Q1: 5823.0
Q3: 12054.0
IQR: 6231.0
Lower Limit: -3523.5
Upper Limit: 21400.5

# Identify outliers using the IQR limits already computed

Purpose: To identify the distribution of purchase amounts and detect potential outliers.

Histogram: Shows how purchase values are distributed.

Q1 & Q3: Show the middle 50% of purchase values.

Upper Limit: Helps identify unusually high purchases.

KDE line: Shows the overall shape of the distribution.

Conclusion: Most purchases are within the normal range, while values above 21,400 can be considered potential outliers.

In [24]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))

sns.boxplot(x=df["Purchase"])

plt.axvline(
    upper_limit,
    linestyle="--",
    label=f"Upper Limit = {upper_limit:.0f}"
)

plt.title("Purchase Amount - Outlier Detection")
plt.xlabel("Purchase Amount")
plt.legend()

plt.show()

Purpose: To identify and visualize outliers in purchase amounts.

Boxplot: Shows the spread of purchase values.

Blue dashed line: Represents the upper limit of 21,400.

Dots after the limit: Represent potential outliers.

Conclusion: Most purchases are within the normal range, while purchases above 21,400 are potential outliers.

The IQR method identified several extreme purchase values. Further investigation shows that these values represent valid transactions rather than data-entry errors. Therefore, the outliers were retained for analysis to avoid removing genuine high-value purchases.

Customer Demographic Analysis¶

In [33]:
customer_transactions = (
    df.groupby("User_ID").size().reset_index(name="Items_Purchased")
)

print(f"Average items purchased per customer: {customer_transactions['Items_Purchased'].mean():.1f}")
print(f"Median items purchased per customer: {customer_transactions['Items_Purchased'].median():.0f}")
print(f"Min items: {customer_transactions['Items_Purchased'].min()}, Max items: {customer_transactions['Items_Purchased'].max()}")

# Distribution view — more useful than a single "repeat rate" number
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
sns.histplot(customer_transactions["Items_Purchased"], bins=50)
plt.title("Distribution of Items Purchased per Customer")
plt.xlabel("Number of Items Purchased")
plt.ylabel("Number of Customers")
plt.show()

Average items purchased per customer: 93.4
Median items purchased per customer: 54
Min items: 6, Max items: 1026

This dataset records individual line items, not separate checkout sessions — so nearly every customer will appear multiple times regardless of loyalty.

A "repeat purchase rate" isn't meaningful here without an order ID or timestamp.

Instead, we look at items purchased per customer: average of 93.4, median of 54 — showing most customers bought a handful of items in this Black Friday period, with a long tail of high-volume shoppers.

Customer-Level Analysis¶

In [45]:
customer_clv = (
    df.groupby("User_ID")
    .agg(Total_Purchase=("Purchase", "sum"), Number_of_Transactions=("Purchase", "count"))
    .reset_index()
)

# Avg order value — spend per line item, NOT lifetime value
customer_clv["Avg_Order_Value"] = customer_clv["Total_Purchase"] / customer_clv["Number_of_Transactions"]

customer_clv.head()
Out[45]:
User_ID Total_Purchase Number_of_Transactions Avg_Order_Value
0 1000001 334093 35 9545.514286
1 1000002 810472 77 10525.610390
2 1000003 341635 29 11780.517241
3 1000004 206468 14 14747.714286
4 1000005 821001 106 7745.292453

This dataset has no transaction date, so a projected CLV can't be calculated.

Total_Purchase is used here as a CLV proxy (cumulative spend to date).

Avg_Order_Value is a separate metric — average spend per line item, not lifetime value.

Cross-Selling Analysis¶

It identifies which products are often purchased together.

This helps businesses recommend related products and increase sales.

In [55]:
# Cross-Selling Analysis

valid_df = df[df["Product_Category_2"] != "Unknown"]

cross_sell = (
    valid_df
    .groupby(["Product_Category_1", "Product_Category_2"])
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="Number_of_Purchases")
    .sort_values("Number_of_Purchases", ascending=False)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

cross_sell["Purchase_Percentage"] = (
    cross_sell["Number_of_Purchases"] / len(valid_df) * 100
).round(2)

“Product category 1 + 2 is the most common combination, accounting for 13.07% of purchases.

This shows customers frequently buy these two categories together, making them a good combination for cross-selling and bundle offers.”

Product Category 3 contains a high proportion of missing values (approximately 70%). Therefore, it is retained for completeness but is not prioritized in cross-selling analysis. Product Category 1 and Product Category 2 provide more reliable coverage for identifying common product combinations.

# Encode Age ordinally so it can be used in correlation
age_order = {
    "0-17": 0, "18-25": 1, "26-35": 2, "36-45": 3,
    "46-50": 4, "51-55": 5, "55+": 6
}
df["Age_Ordinal"] = df["Age"].map(age_order)

# Select meaningful numerical variables
corr_data = df[["Age_Ordinal", "Occupation", "Stay_Years", "Purchase"]]

# Calculate correlation
correlation_matrix = corr_data.corr()

# Plot correlation heatmap
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(correlation_matrix, annot=True, cmap="coolwarm", fmt=".2f")
plt.title("Correlation Heatmap: Demographics vs Purchase")
plt.xlabel("Variables")
plt.ylabel("Variables")
plt.show()

None of the demographic variables show a meaningful linear relationship with Purchase:

Age_Ordinal (0.02), Occupation (0.02), and Stay_Years (0.01) are all effectively zero.

Age and Occupation show a weak relationship with each other (0.09), but neither correlates with spend.

Statistical Hypothesis Testing¶

“Statistical hypothesis testing helps us determine whether the observed differences in purchase behavior are statistically significant.”

Gender H0

There is no significant difference in purchase between males and females.

H1

There is a significant difference.

In [66]:
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

# Purchase values for male customers
male = df[df["Gender"] == "M"]["Purchase"]

# Purchase values for female customers
female = df[df["Gender"] == "F"]["Purchase"]

# Independent t-test
t_stat, p_value = ttest_ind(male, female)

print("t_stat:", round(t_stat, 2))
print("p_value:", p_value)

# Decision
if p_value < 0.05:
    print("Reject H0: There is a significant difference in average purchase between male and female customers.")
else:
    print("Fail to reject H0: There is no significant difference in average purchase between male and female customers.")

t_stat: 44.84
p_value: 0.0
Reject H0: There is a significant difference in average purchase between male and female customers.

“Since the p-value is 0.0 (< 0.05), we reject H₀. There is a significant difference in average purchase between male and female customers.”

Marital Status Hypothesis Test¶

In [67]:
single=df[df["Marital_Status"]==0]["Purchase"]
married=df[df["Marital_Status"]==1]["Purchase"]

t_stat,p_value=ttest_ind(single,married)

print("t_stat:",round((t_stat),2))
print("p_value:",round((p_value),2))

if p_value < 0.05:
    print("Reject H0")
    print("There is a significant difference in average purchase between single and married customers")
else:
    print("Fail to Reject H0")
    print("There is no significant difference in average purchase between single and married customers")

t_stat: 0.34
p_value: 0.73
Fail to Reject H0
There is no significant difference in average purchase between single and married customers

“Since the p-value is 0.73 (> 0.05), we fail to reject H₀. There is no significant difference in average purchase between single and married customers.”

ANOVA — City

In [68]:
city_A=  df[df["City_Category"]=="A"]["Purchase"]
city_B=  df[df["City_Category"]=="B"]["Purchase"]
city_c=  df[df["City_Category"]=="C"]["Purchase"]

f_stat,p_value=stats.f_oneway(city_A,city_B,city_c)

print("f_stat:",f_stat)
print("p_value:",p_value)


if p_value < 0.05:
    print("Reject H0")
    print("There is a significant difference in average purchase among the city categories.")
else:
    print("Fail to Reject H0")
    print("There is no significant difference in average purchase among the city categories.")

f_stat: 1130.7459610102974
p_value: 0.0
Reject H0
There is a significant difference in average purchase among the city categories.

“Since the p-value is 0.0 (< 0.05), we reject H₀. There is a significant difference in average purchase among the three city categories.”

ANOVA — Age Groups¶

In [69]:
age_groups = [
    df[df["Age"] == age]["Purchase"]
    for age in df["Age"].unique()
]

f_stat, p_value = stats.f_oneway(*age_groups)

print("F-statistic:", f_stat)
print("P-value:", p_value)

F-statistic: 40.57579909450408
P-value: 1.0535639392516708e-49

“Since the p-value is very small (< 0.05), we reject H₀. Average purchase differs significantly across age groups.”

Final Business Insights

26–35 age group is the largest customer segment.

City B has the highest number of transactions.

Male customers dominate transactions and purchase value.

Some product categories generate higher revenue than others.

High-value customers contribute significantly to total revenue.

Gender has a significant impact on purchase behavior.

Marital status has no significant impact on average purchase.

Some product categories are frequently purchased together, creating cross-selling opportunities.

Business Recommendations

  • Target the 26–35 age group with personalized offers and campaigns, as they form the largest customer segment.

  • Focus marketing efforts on City B to strengthen sales in the highest-transaction market.

  • Target male customers with relevant promotions, while also creating campaigns to increase female customer participation.

  • Promote high-revenue product categories through discounts, featured placements, and targeted campaigns.

  • Retain high-value customers using loyalty programs, exclusive offers, and personalized recommendations.

  • Use gender-based purchase insights to create more targeted marketing strategies, as purchase behavior differs significantly by gender.

  • Avoid heavily segmenting offers by marital status, since it does not significantly affect average purchase value.

  • Create bundle offers for frequently purchased product combinations to increase cross-selling and average order value.

Overall Recommendation

“Focus on high-performing customer segments, cities, and products while using personalized promotions and cross-selling strategies to increase sales and customer value.”

Recommendation 1 — Target high-value customers

Create loyalty offers for customers in the High Value segment.

Recommendation 2 — Gender-based campaigns

Since your hypothesis test shows a significant gender difference, consider differentiated campaigns.

Recommendation 3 — Focus on high-performing products

Promote products/categories generating the highest revenue.

Recommendation 4 — Cross-selling

Bundle frequently purchased product categories.

Recommendation 5 — City-specific marketing

Use city-level purchase behavior to create targeted campaigns.
